title: Walking between
tomorrow: why did desert monks call the afternoon a demon?

cards: The walk back from lunch usually happens on fast-forward: head down, already inside the next task, half-jogging to be on time. A companion of the Prophet named Abu Qatada remembers a day when some people ran.
They were praying behind the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, when he heard a commotion: latecomers hurrying to catch up. When the prayer ended, he turned and asked what all that noise had been.
We were rushing to the prayer, they said. Late, and eager to make it. His answer was about their feet.

teach.b: Don't do that, he told them. When you come to the prayer, come with calm. Pray what you catch with everyone, and complete what you missed.
In another saying he puts it as a pair: walk to the prayer with calm and with dignity, and don't hurry.

The Arabic word for that calm is sakina, a settled stillness, and in the Qur'an it's the name of a peace God sends down into believers' hearts. So the Prophet asked for that peace in the walking, not only in the prayer.
Here is the teaching, named plainly. In Islam, the walk to prayer already belongs to the worship.
Another hadith in Bukhari says that whoever washes for prayer and walks to the mosque for nothing but the prayer is raised a degree with each step, and a sin is taken away. The steps count.
That's why the teaching is to walk to the mosque calmly, even when the prayer has already begun. Running would spend the walk to save a minute. Notice what the Prophet didn't say.
He didn't say be late, or stay home. Getting there mattered.

teach.h: THE WALK BELONGS TO WHERE YOU'RE GOING.
teach.b: He said the in-between is part of where you're going, so walk it with calm. The Qur'an describes the servants of the Merciful as people who walk upon the earth gently, and answer the foolish with peace.
On your own path, with the tag left on: the walk between two things isn't dead time to rush through. It's a short path of its own.
Something to tell a friend tonight: told about people running late, the Prophet didn't say hurry. He said come with calm.

how: Muslims are taught to walk to the mosque calmly rather than run, even when the prayer has begun, joining what they catch and completing the rest; the hadith counts each step taken toward prayer.

o: the walk from one task to the next, done with calm
a long hike taken on weekends to clear your head
the wasted gap of time between two meetings

games.q: walking to prayer: tap the pairs.
p: raised a degree, a sin taken away

s: if you're late for prayer, running shows you care
the Prophet told the ones who rushed: come with calm, pray what you catch, complete the rest.
in the hadith, the steps toward prayer are counted
each step raises a degree and takes a sin away.
the Prophet told the latecomers they might as well stay home
he told them to come, calmly, and complete what they missed.

games.q: your friend sprints between back-to-back classes and walks in too frazzled to hear the first ten minutes. what fits the Prophet's word to the ones who ran?
o: walk the in-between with calm: it's part of where she's going, and she can catch up after.
sprint harder; arriving on time is the only thing that counts.
skip any class she'd be late for; better absent than late.
games.why: the Prophet didn't say stay away, and he didn't say run. come with calm, catch what you can, complete the rest.

practice: Stand and walk slowly across the room and back, a few steps each way, with the calm the Prophet asked for on the way to prayer. Feel each foot lift and land.
If a rush rises in you, let the next step be a little slower than the last. At each end, pause, turn, and begin again.

wordCard.voice: Walking between: the walk from one thing to the next, done with calm. In Islam, the walk to prayer is part of the prayer, every step counted.

orig.note: Arabic: calm, a settled peace; the Prophet asked for it on the walk to prayer.

carryVoice: Carry this one: between, the walk from one thing to the next, done with calm, every step counted. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 635 (Abu Qatada: the noise of people hurrying; 'come to the prayer with calm; pray what you catch and complete what you missed')
Sahih al-Bukhari 636 (go to the prayer with calm and dignity, and do not hurry)
Sahih al-Bukhari 647 (walking to the mosque for the prayer alone: each step raises a degree and removes a sin)
Qur'an 48:4 (God sent down the sakina, peace of reassurance, into the hearts of the believers)
Qur'an 25:63 (the servants of the Merciful walk upon the earth gently and answer the foolish with peace)
